title: From predictor to assistant
objectives: Explain how fine-tuning on example conversations turns a text predictor into an assistant.

screens.prose: The same request goes to two models. One has only been pretrained; the other was trained further. Both replies are invented examples.

lines: You: Write a polite email asking for a refund.
Model A: Write a polite email asking for a discount. Write a polite email asking for a meeting. Write a short note thanking a colleague.
params.title: Model A (an invented example)

lines: You: Write a polite email asking for a refund.
Model B: Dear Customer Services, I bought a kettle from you on 3 March. It stopped working after a week. Please could you refund the £35 I paid? Thank you for your help. Yours faithfully, Sam
params.title: Model B (an invented example)

screens.question: Tap the reply that does what was asked.

hints.text: Which reply is an email?
One reply starts "Dear".
Model B writes the email. Model A writes more lines like yours.

feedback.correct: Model B wrote the email. Model A treated your request as the first line of a list of tasks.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the reply that is an email asking for a refund.

byKey.left: Model A continued a list of writing tasks, which is likely text after such a line. It never wrote the email.

explain.text: Model A is a base model: a line like yours often opens a list of writing tasks, so it wrote more tasks. Model B was trained further on example conversations, so a helpful reply is its likely next text.

screens.prose: Here is how Model B was made. Slide to add the second stage to the first.

state.caption: Stage 1: pretraining turns web text into a base model.

frames.caption: Stage 1: pretraining turns web text into a base model.
Stage 2: fine-tuning on example chats turns the base model into an assistant.

screens.question: What does the second stage train the base model on?

options.text: Many example conversations written by people
More web text of the same kind as before
options.why: Slide to stage 2. The new input is example chats, not more web text.

options.text: A list of true facts to learn by heart
options.why: There is no list of facts in either stage.

options.text: The emails of the people who later use it
options.why: Fine-tuning chats are written by people hired to show good replies, not taken from this assistant's users.

hints.text: Slide to stage 2. What new box feeds fine-tuning?
Look at the box on the left of stage 2.
Example chats and the base model both feed fine-tuning.

feedback.correct: Example chats: each shows a request and the kind of reply wanted.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to stage 2 and read the box that feeds fine-tuning.

explain.text: Stage 2 starts from the base model and trains it further on example chats. Each chat shows a request followed by a good reply, written by a person.

canvas.caption: Stage 2: fine-tuning on example chats turns the base model into an assistant.

screens.prose: Here is one example chat. People write a great many like it, each a request and a good reply. Training the base model further on them is **fine-tuning**, and its result is an **assistant**.

rows: Can you explain what a bond is?
A bond is a loan you make to a government or a firm. They pay you interest, then repay the loan on a set date.

screens.question: After fine-tuning on many such chats, what is the likely next text after a request?

options.text: A helpful reply in the style of the examples
More requests, as in a list of requests
options.why: That was the base model's habit. Fine-tuning made a reply the likely next text.

options.text: An exact copy of one example reply
options.why: It learns the pattern of replies, not one reply to copy; your request differs from every example.

options.text: Whatever came next in the web text
options.why: Fine-tuning moved it on from the web text: after a request, a reply is now likely.

hints.text: In the examples, what always follows a request?
Read the second row.
Every example has a reply after the request, so a reply becomes the likely next text.

feedback.correct: A reply in the style of the examples is now the likely next text.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what always follows a request in the examples.

explain.text: Fine-tuning uses the same training as pretraining: predict the next token, lower the error. Only the text changes: now it is requests followed by good replies. So a good reply becomes the likely next text.

screens.prose: Put the making of an assistant in order. The example chats can be written at any time before they are used.
screens.question: Put the steps in the order they happen.

lines.text: Gather a huge body of text from the web
Pretrain: predict the next token, over and over
Get a base model that continues text
Fine-tune the base model on the example chats
Get an assistant that replies to requests

hints.text: What has to exist before anything can be pretrained?
Follow the arrows in the diagram.
Text, pretraining, base model; then fine-tuning needs the base model and the chats; the assistant comes last.

feedback.correct: Text, pretraining, base model; then fine-tuning on the chats gives the assistant.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the arrows: each step needs the steps that feed it.

byKey.w2: Pretraining needs the text first. Gather the web text before you pretrain.
byKey.w3: The base model is what pretraining produces, so it comes after pretraining.
byKey.w5: Fine-tuning needs both the base model and the example chats, so it comes after both.
byKey.w6: The assistant is the result of fine-tuning, so it comes last.

explain.text: Each step needs what feeds it: text before pretraining, a base model before fine-tuning, and the chats before they are used. The assistant is the last thing made.

screens.prose: A team is choosing example chats. They want the assistant to say it does not know when it cannot know.

rows: What will the FTSE 100 close at tomorrow?
What will the FTSE 100 close at tomorrow?
I cannot know tomorrow's close. I can explain what moves the index.

screens.question: Tap the example that would teach the assistant to say it does not know when it should.

hints.text: Which request has no answer anyone could know today?
Two examples ask about tomorrow.
Of the two, pick the reply that admits it cannot know.

feedback.correct: Example B shows a question with no knowable answer and a reply that says so.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the reply that admits it cannot know.

byKey.r0: Example A answers a question no one can answer, and sounds sure. Training on it teaches guessing.
byKey.r2: Example C is a good reply, but its question has an answer. It teaches nothing about doubt.

explain.text: Example B pairs an unknowable question with a reply that says so. Fine-tuning copies the habits in its examples, so chats like B are how an assistant learns to admit doubt.

screens.prose: Another team fine-tunes on examples where every reply is confident. None says "I am not sure", even where no one could know.

rows: Will this share rise next week?
What was the firm's profit last year?
Which fund is best for me?
Fund K is the best for you.

screens.question: What habit does this assistant most likely learn?

options.text: To answer confidently even when it cannot know
To admit doubt on hard questions
options.why: None of the examples shows doubt, so nothing teaches it.

options.text: To refuse questions about the future
options.why: Example A answers a question about the future. That is the habit it copies.

options.text: To check its answers before replying
options.why: Nothing in the examples shows checking. Fine-tuning copies what the examples show.

hints.text: Does any example reply show doubt?
Example A answers a question about next week.
Every reply sounds sure, so sounding sure is the habit learned.

feedback.correct: It learns to sound sure every time, because every example did.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what all three replies have in common.

explain.text: All three replies sound sure, including one about the future that no one can know. Fine-tuning copies that habit. An assistant trained this way states guesses as if they were facts.

screens.prose: A team fine-tunes a base model on a large set of polite example chats about many topics. A colleague says: "Now it knows far more facts."

rows: A huge body of web text

screens.question: What does fine-tuning mostly change?

options.text: How it replies: its style and its habits
The facts it knows, which grow a great deal
options.why: You gave fine-tuning the job of teaching facts. Next to the web text the chats are small, so they mostly teach how to reply.

options.text: The size of the network, which grows
options.why: Fine-tuning trains the same network further; it does not make it bigger.

options.text: Nothing, since it is the same network
options.why: It is the same network, but its replies change a lot, as Model B showed.

hints.text: Which stage reads far more text?
Compare the last column.
The facts it can use come mostly from the enormous web text. The chats mostly teach how to reply.

feedback.correct: Fine-tuning mostly changes the style and the habits. Most of what it knows came from pretraining.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare how much text each stage learns from.

byKey.facts: You expected the chats to add knowledge. Next to the web text they are small, so they mostly change the style and habits; the facts come mostly from pretraining.

explain.text: Pretraining reads an enormous body of text, the source of most of what the model can say. Fine-tuning's chats are few by comparison. They change how it replies, not mainly what it knows.

screens.prose: The two stages together: $$\text{base model} \xrightarrow{\text{example chats}} \text{assistant}$$ Pretraining supplies most of what it can say. Fine-tuning shapes how it replies, good habits and bad.
screens.question: A new assistant replies in a cheerful style and uses many facts. Where does each mostly come from?

options.text: The style from fine-tuning, most facts from pretraining
Both the style and the facts from fine-tuning
options.why: The chats are small next to the web text, so they give the style more than the facts.

options.text: The style from pretraining, the facts from fine-tuning
options.why: That is the wrong way round. Web text gives most facts; the chats give the style.

options.text: Both from the request the user typed
options.why: The request is one line. The style and facts were learned in training.

feedback.correct: The style from the example chats, most facts from the web text.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall which stage reads the huge body of text.

screens.prose: A bank fine-tunes a model on years of its agents' chats with customers. Since then, its late-payment fee has changed from £12 to £15. The bank and chats are invented.

rows: How do I reset my card PIN?
I can help with that. You can reset it in the app, under card settings.
What is the fee for a late payment?
I am sorry, I cannot approve loans in a chat. I can tell you how to apply.

screens.question: Select all that apply: what is the new assistant likely to copy from the chats?

options.text: The agents' polite, helpful tone
Saying it cannot approve loans in a chat
The old £12 fee, which is now out of date
The new £15 fee
options.why: The chats were written before the change. Fine-tuning copies what its examples say, out of date or not.

options.text: A view of each customer's account
options.why: Training on chats gives it habits of text, not a link to the bank's systems.

hints.text: Fine-tuning copies what the examples show. What do they show?
Read the reply about the fee.
Tone, the honest answer about loans and the £12 fee are all in the chats. The £15 fee is not.

feedback.correct: It copies the habits in the chats, good and bad: the tone, the honest loan answer and the old fee.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick only what appears in the example chats.

explain.text: Fine-tuning copies the habits in its examples, good and bad. The tone and the honest "I cannot approve loans" carry over, and so does the old fee: a fact repeated across many chats can be copied, so out-of-date examples are dangerous. The bank has to check its examples, not just collect them.

ideas: Fine-tuning trains a base model further on example chats written by people: a request, then a good reply.
It is the same training as pretraining, on different text, so a helpful reply becomes the likely next text. The result is an assistant.
Fine-tuning mostly changes style and habits, good and bad; most of what the model can say comes from pretraining.

formula.name: Fine-tuning
formula.note: It copies the habits in its examples.

summary.trap: Fine-tuning does not mainly add facts. It changes how the model replies.

quiz.question: What does fine-tuning train a base model on?

options.text: Example conversations written by people
More of the same web text
options.why: More web text would only make a better base model. Fine-tuning uses example chats.

options.text: People's rankings of pairs of replies
options.why: Rankings are used in the next stage, in l3.

options.text: A list of checked facts
options.why: Neither stage uses a list of facts.

feedback.correct: Example conversations: a request, then a good reply.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the box that feeds fine-tuning.

explain.text: Fine-tuning trains the base model further on example conversations that people wrote. Each shows a request and a good reply, so a reply becomes the likely next text.

quiz.question: Why does a base model often answer a request by writing more requests?

options.text: In web text, lines like that often come in lists
It was trained to ignore requests
options.why: Nothing trained it to ignore anything. It writes likely text.

options.text: It is broken and needs repair
options.why: It works as trained: it continues text.

options.text: The request was not clear enough
options.why: A clear request gets the same treatment: it is continued, not answered.

feedback.correct: A request often opens a list, so more list lines are likely text.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what a base model does with any text.

explain.text: A base model continues text. On the web, a line like a request often opens a list of such lines. So more of them is the likely continuation.

quiz.question: You want an assistant to say "I am not sure" when it should. What do you add to its fine-tuning examples?

options.text: Examples where the good reply admits doubt
More web text about uncertainty
options.why: Web text changes the base model. The habit of a reply is taught by example chats.

options.text: More examples of confident replies
options.why: Confident examples teach confidence, the opposite of what you want.

options.text: Nothing: it will learn doubt by itself
options.why: Fine-tuning copies what the examples show. Doubt must be in them.

feedback.correct: Examples that show doubt teach the habit of doubt.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fine-tuning copies the habits in its examples.

explain.text: Fine-tuning copies habits from its examples. To get an honest "I am not sure", put examples in which the good reply says so.

quiz.question: A model is fine-tuned on a small set of medical chats written in a kind tone. What mostly changes?

options.text: Its replies sound kinder; its medical knowledge grows little
It now knows as much as a doctor
options.why: A small set of chats teaches a style. Knowledge comes mostly from pretraining.

options.text: Nothing changes at all
options.why: The tone of its replies changes, as the examples teach.

options.text: It learns the facts in the chats and keeps its old tone
options.why: It is the other way round: the style is what a small set of chats mostly changes.

feedback.correct: Mostly the tone. The knowledge came mostly from pretraining.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what fine-tuning mostly changes.

explain.text: A small set of chats mostly teaches how to reply. Its tone becomes kinder, while what it can say about medicine comes mostly from pretraining.
